doc.title: Jimmy and Jeannie Cheatham interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 12, 1998

title: The blues as universal spirit music
summary: On why the blues is endlessly usable; an African man in robes calls their playing 'spirit music'; blues will spread worldwide.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: What the blues is, and why every jazz player needs it

blocks.x: What is it that — this is probably an unanswerable question, but — the blues has been so much a part, it is a music in itself, but also giving rise to rock & roll, and being so much a part of jazz music. I’ve always been fascinated by the blues as a form of music that allows so much to be done with it, over and over and over. That the form is so inevitable, you can always feel where you are, and maybe that’s one of the beauties of it.
Maybe that is.
Yeah. And the simplicity of it.
Here we go again, simplicity.

Simplicity, and the way it falls you see, no matter how the melody goes, but in terms of dealing with the progression, you know, fundamentally, it’s symmetrical. Perfectly symmetrical. There’s no chord that jerks you around and on a wrong beat.
No. No Stravinsky there.
Yeah. It just leads you right into the next thing.
And it’s so comforting.

Because they are statements. It’s like telling a story, you know, telling a story you see. And so it’s all there. It’s like talking all the time. A conversation. And like speaking on behalf of the grooves, in terms of expression, there is not one act of emotion or intellect, you just name it, that deals with life on this planet earth, that can’t be expressed with the blues.

With the blues. It’s like they say Shakespeare only had twelve stories, but that he was sort of like an astrologer, the twelve different signs you know, and each one has its own characteristics. So you could really—
Back to the twelve again.
I think we’re on to something here.
You’d better believe it.

Well actually he said it’s all universal. But that’s what makes it so wonderful about the blues, it’s universal and you could take it anywhere. You can take it to China, you can take it to BongBong, Africa. People will stop.
And they recognize it.
And they recognize it.
Because they call it spirit music.

We were playing at the Sheraton, upstairs at the bar, and this African came in, he had on a suit, a three-piece suit. He stood there for a minute, and he went back upstairs and he came back in his robe. The whole regalia. He says, “I must address you.” He says, “You are playing spirit music.” And he sat down. © Fillius Jazz Archive -23-
That’s exactly what he said.
So help me. And I said to myself, ohh. So we kept playing. But that’s how much he gave to it. He went up and had to re-dress.

And to have that experience was an affirmation, a confirmation of what is. Whether we understand it totally or not, but it’s a confirmation, whatever we realize that it is — but it helps to expand us and keep going. That’s what’s talking about the faith you know, to help sustain and maintain they call it.
That was a real experience.

To get to the next one. That’s right. It’s really something. And now that we naturally, via high tech communications and everything, and naturally you hear on mass consciousness about global observations etcetera you know, and the whole bit. But it’s going to be interesting. We’re going to hear some blues to come out of China, Japan, all over the world, Turkey, it doesn’t make any difference, India, it doesn’t make any difference.
I think so too.
And you’re going to hear a reminiscent aspect of the blues.
A Muddy Water fan.
It has to go on the great list of twentieth century inventions, doesn’t it?
Oh I think so.
The blues? Oh yeah.
Let’s say nineteenth and twentieth.
But, yeah that’s true, but in reality, it’s always been here. Really.
